Learning Objectives
Review the basic concepts of radiography.
Discuss the invaluable role of radiography in orthopaedics.
Identify factors that affect patient irradiation dose to decrease the risk of irradiation-induced
complications.
Explain specialized radiographic views and techniques to evaluate for specific pathologies.
Review the utility of fluoroscopy in orthopaedic procedures.
Principles of Radiography
Radiographs are obtained by projecting x-ray beams through an object onto film or an image
detector.

The image produced is a two-dimensional projectional map of the amount of irradiation not
absorbed by the object along the course of the x- ray beam.
Similar to photography, the lightness or darkness of the image is determined by how much
irradiation moves through the object and to the film/detector (exposure).
The lightness/darkness is affected by the radiodensity and thickness of the object.
The denser the object (eg, metal or bone), the more the irradiation is absorbed; therefore, the
object appears lighter or whiter (less exposed film). Less dense objects (eg, air and fat) are
radiolucent and appear dark on radiographs (more exposed film).
Qualified technologists obtain radiographs.

Principles of Radiography
Attenuation refers to the reduction of the intensity of an x-ray beam as the beam
photons pass through a specific object (confusingly called the subject of the image). The
greater the density and thickness of an object, the more that object will attenuate x-rays.
Therefore, bones and metal implants, which have high mass density, appear whiter on
images than soft tissues or plastic implants.
Subject contrast refers to the difference in attenuation between a radiographic object
and its background based on the object’s composition. A great amount of contrast exists
between bone and its surrounding muscle, making the bone quite visible.
Radiographs can be obtained by using film or an image detector. If an image detector is
used, the resulting image is digital and can be stored and manipulated as a digital
dataset. The digital format allows images to be portable and transferable via
electronic/computer communication, compact disks, and other digital formats. Images
typically are stored on a picture archiving and communication system.1
Advantages
Available, inexpensive, fast
Helps guide subsequent imaging studies

Specialized views and positions can be obtained.
Real-time radiography, or fluoroscopy, can be performed.

Advantages
Radiography is the most commonly used medical imaging modality because it is a readily
available, non-invasive, low-cost, fast form of imaging familiar to medical professionals.
Most physicians interpret radiographs as part of their practice. Although imaging
artifacts occur, most do not prohibit basic interpretation2 (Resource 1). In addition, the
spatial resolution of radiography exceeds that of cross-sectional imaging modalities (ie,
ultrasonography, CT, and MRI).
Digital radiographs are the main diagnostic and initial imaging studies for most
orthopaedic surgery patients. Radiography allows for detailed interpretation of the
bones and, therefore, is heavily used for arthritis characterization; fracture detection and
follow-up; bone tumor evaluation; preoperative planning (Videos 1 and 2); and simple
measurements, such as in patients with skeletal dysplasia, limb-length discrepancy, or
scoliosis. Because of inherent magnification, a calibration ball or a ruler is placed at the
midpoint of the patient for exact measurements. Calibration balls also are useful for
templating implants. Radiography usually is sufficient to establish the diagnosis of the
aforementioned entities, and additional imaging modalities often are unnecessary. In
patients with chronic back pain that warrants imaging, radiographs are the appropriate
initial imaging study according to the American College of Radiology Appropriateness
Criteria3 (Resource 2). For most other musculoskeletal indications, radiographs are
considered the appropriate initial imaging study according to the American College of
Radiology. Follow-up of musculoskeletal disease also typically is performed via
radiographs.

Despite technological advancements, radiography remains the mainstay initial imaging
modality for the evaluation of primary bone and soft-tissue tumors, irrespective of lesion
location or patient age4,5 (Resources 3 and 4). Many important findings can be
ascertained from radiographs, upholding the classic teaching that patient age and the
radiographic appearance of a lesion most closely predict the pathologic diagnosis.
Radiographs depict lesion location, matrix, zone of transition, periosteal reaction,
associated soft-tissue mass and calcification, and pathologic fracture (Video 2). In
addition, radiography is useful in directing subsequent imaging studies, with soft-tissue
masses often evaluated via ultrasonography and aggressive osseous neoplasms often
evaluated via MRI. Radiography also is the first imaging modality for surveillance after
primary bone tumor resection.
Special techniques, positions, and equipment in radiography can be used to obtain
specific information. Stress maneuvers are performed to detect joint instability. For
example, oblique stress views of the ankle after trauma are used to evaluate the medial
clear space to assess for deltoid ligament injury. Weight-bearing views also are useful in
many circumstances, such as in the evaluation of pes planus and hallux valgus
deformities, equivocal Lisfranc injury, and limb alignment. Weight-bearing views allow
for evaluation of joint space narrowing, such as in patients with hip or knee
osteoarthritis6 (Resource 5). Stitching software creates a continuous long image, which is
useful to evaluate scoliosis and leg lengths. Specific filters can be used to enhance image
quality; for example, a gradient filter optimizes visualization of the toes and heel on foot
radiographs.
Routine radiographic views of various bones and joints are summarized in Table 1.2
Myriad specialized radiographic views exist and can be obtained in addition to basic AP,
lateral, and oblique views of the extremities to determine specific information. Examples
of specialized radiographic views pertaining to the shoulder are summarized in

In imaging the shoulder, various projections can be obtained to evaluate suspected
abnormalities involving the glenohumeral, acromioclavicular, sternoclavicular, and
scapulothoracic joints7 (Resource 7). Knowledge of the advantages and disadvantages of
standard views optimizes radiographic evaluation.
Disadvantages
Irradiation is transmitted to the patient. Irradiation is a risk, especially to an early developing
fetus.
Radiography is not effective for soft-tissue imaging because of poor contrast resolution.
Radiographs are always magnified; however, measurement standards can be placed next to
the object to calculate the magnification.
The quality of radiographs, similar to that of most imaging studies, may be operator-
dependent, and malpositioning or poor exposure may necessitate repeat imaging.

Disadvantages
Although radiography transmits ionizing radiation to the patient, it is an exceptionally
low dose compared with CT, and certain factors can be implemented to ensure the
patient receives the lowest dose possible (but not at the expense of obtaining diagnostic
images). This is the as low as reasonably achievable principle, which states that
irradiation exposure should do better than harm and the dose should be kept as low as
reasonably possible.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Radiography and Fluoroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000502
8/26

Compared with cross-sectional imaging, little subject contrast exists between different
soft tissues on radiography. Unless reactive or destructive changes are present in the
adjacent bone, radiography is of little use in evaluating most soft-tissue findings at the
joints. For example, articular cartilage loss cannot be detected on radiographs until
cartilage loss is advanced enough to cause joint space narrowing. Similarly, unossified
epiphyses cannot be observed on radiographs unless secondary signs of injury are
present, and soft-tissue spine injuries, such as disk protrusions, are not visible on
radiographs.2
Although the amount of contrast observed between bone and soft tissue on radiographs
is high, bone radiographs may be limited in certain circumstances. For example, for
disease that are primarily in the medullary cavity of the mid-diaphyses of long bones,
findings may be missed because trabeculae are sparse in this location. Radiography also
plays a limited role in assessing treatment response in patients with malignant osseous
lesions because bone tumors typically increase in density and size after chemotherapy
secondary to remodeling and healing (Video 2).
Because x-ray beams diverge as they leave the source, the projected image of an object
is always larger than the actual object. Therefore, measurements of length on a
radiograph are calibrated to a physical standard that is placed adjacent to the patient at
the time the image is obtained. Failure to include the physical standard may result in
overestimation of fracture length, fragment size, or template size. Enlargement also may
be advantageous in certain circumstances, such as in magnification radiography of
arthritic hands.2
Magnification commonly occurs if the patient is close to the x-ray source, resulting in
image blurring. Magnification also occurs if the object being imaged is far from the
detector. Magnification can be reduced by increasing the distance from the x-ray source
to the object being imaged and by placing the object being imaged next to the detector.
According to the inverse square law, which states that dose decreases by the square of
the distance from the x-ray source, moving the patient farther from the source will
decrease not only magnification but also irradiation exposure8 (Figure 1). Therefore,
radiographs obtained via portable units tend to be of inferior quality and highly

magnified.
Figure 1 Schematic illustrations show the effect of geometric magnification on entrance
skin dose. With fixed source-to-image receptor distance, magnification and skin entrance
exposure (SEE) increase as the patient is moved closer to the x-ray source. (Reproduced
with permission from Mahesh M: Fluoroscopy: Patient radiation exposure issues.
Radiographics 2001;21[4]:1033-1045.)
X-ray technicians undergo rigorous training and are examined and certified by the
American Registry of Radiologic Technologists. Physicians rely on the skills of x-ray
technologists to produce radiographs; however, they are responsible for obtaining
complete, superior quality imaging studies. Inadequate imaging studies may result if
only a single view is obtained, patient positioning is improper, or the field of view is
inadequate. Overlapping structures on radiographs can be obscured, and obtaining
orthogonal views is not always feasible. Even with orthogonal views, subtle findings may
be masked in the presence of overlapping cast material.
Although the availability and rapidity of radiography typically are considered advantages,
these factors also may lead to over-imaging. For example, a study on the utility of post-

mobilization imaging in patients with a nonsurgical pelvic ring injury found that these
radiographs were of limited value and that eliminating this step would decrease costs
and irradiation exposure9 (Resource 8).
Fluoroscopy
Real-time radiographic imaging, or fluoroscopy, allows for instantaneous feedback while
obtaining stress radiographs, during angiography, and during orthopaedic procedures.

Fluoroscopy
Fluoroscopy can be thought of as continuous radiographic images being transmitted to a
monitor so that movement of a body part, contrast dye, or implant can be observed in
real time. Because of the high frame rate of 25 to 30 frames per second, frame-to-frame
variation cannot be distinguished, and motion appears continuous to the human eye.
The fluoroscopic unit consists of an x-ray tube, collimator, anti-scatter grid, image
receptor, image processing computer, and display monitor10 (Figure 2). The x-ray image
intensifier, or flat panel detector, is used to convert the x-rays emerging from the patient
into an image. Fluoroscopic images have an inverted grayscale compared with standard
radiographs, meaning dense structures (eg, bones) appear dark/black on fluoroscopic
images.

C-arms are mobile image intensifier systems frequently used in orthopaedic surgery.11
(Resource 9). The C-arm unit can be rotated axially and sagittally around the patient on
the surgical table to obtain frontal and lateral views10 (Figure 3).

Advantages
Fluoroscopy provides real-time images.
Fluoroscopy can be used to create three-dimensional images.

Advantages
Real-time radiographic image production allows for dynamic evaluation and
instantaneous feedback, which is particularly useful to guide surgical management and
orthopaedic trauma management.4
For example, manual closed fracture reduction of the distal radius can be performed
with the use of fluoroscopy (Video 3). With real-time maneuvering and rotation of the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Radiography and Fluoroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000502
13/26

extremity and adjustments of the x-ray beam inclination angle, instantaneous feedback
on fracture stability, ulnar variance, articular alignment can be obtained. Studies have
reported that formal post-reduction radiographs are unnecessary after manipulation of
pediatric wrist and forearm fractures with the use of mini C-arm fluoroscopy, thereby
reducing patient encounter time, costs, and irradiation exposure12 (Resource 10).
Video 3 Kennedy SA, Cherones AL, Yi A: Distal Radius Fractures: Radiographic Anatomy and

Surgeons, 2019. https://www.aaos.org/videos/video-detail-page/20299__Videos.
Accessed August 10, 2021.
Fluoroscopy is used to guide more minimally invasive procedures, such as arthrography,
joint aspiration, myelography, diskography, nerve injection, lumbar puncture, and
vertebroplasty.
C-arm systems also are heavily used during more involved orthopaedic surgical
procedures. Although technically demanding, percutaneous fixation of the pelvis and
acetabulum performed with the use of fluoroscopy decreases soft-tissue dissection,
blood loss, and surgical time compared with open reduction and internal fixation13
(Resource 11). Fluoroscopic imaging also is useful in arthroplasty to guide the placement
of radiopaque implants. Because of continuous real-time imaging feedback, orthopaedic
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM

surgeons can visualize real-time changes in implant positioning with patient motion. In a
study on the value of intraoperative fluoroscopy in anterior hip arthroplasty, total hip
arthroplasty performed with the use of fluoroscopy more reliably re-created
preoperative femoral offset compared with arthroplasty performed without
fluoroscopy14 (Resource 12).
Fluoroscopy also can be used to align a body part before radiography and to examine
kinematics.
Digital subtraction angiography is a technique that digitally subtracts radiopaque
structures, such as bones, from fluoroscopic images to allow for better delineation of
contrast-opacified vasculature.
The newest fluoroscopy systems have cone beam CT capabilities, in which three-
dimensional images can be obtained by spinning the C-arm around the patient to
perform tomographic reconstruction. Mini C-arm systems are mobile compact units that
are relatively inexpensive, designed for imaging extremities, and associated with low
exposure levels10 (Figure 4).

Disadvantages
The patient and staff are exposed to irradiation during fluoroscopy.
Fluoroscopic images are potentially prone to distortion.
Intraoperative use of fluoroscopy may be associated with a risk for contamination during
surgery.

Disadvantages

Patients and operating room staff are exposed to irradiation during fluoroscopic
imaging. The US FDA mandates the display of the cumulative irradiation dose delivered
from fluoroscopic equipment, which requires close monitoring. Training of operating
personnel is imperative to decrease the time and irradiation necessary for surgical
procedures. C-arm operators must understand the potential effects of irradiation and
the pattern of irradiation distribution from the C-arm. Orthopaedic surgeons should
have knowledge of fluoroscopic methods and a repository of skills that can be used to
reduce irradiation exposure.12
Dose reduction methods similar to those used for radiography can be used for
fluoroscopy8 (Resource 13). Increasing the source-to-skin distance (recall the inverse
square law) while decreasing the patient-to–image-intensifier or flat panel detector
distance is particularly important with the use of C-arm units10 (Figure 5). If x-rays have
a smaller distance to travel to reach the image receptor from the patient, this results in
reduced intraoperative scatter irradiation to the patient and the orthopaedic surgeon15
(Figure 6).
Figure 5 Photographs show two types of equalization filters. These lead-rubber (A) and
lead-acrylic (B) blades are mounted at the collimator, with controls provided to adjust
the blade location and rotation to conform to patient regions of low attenuation.
(Reproduced with permission from Schueler BA: The AAPM/RSNA physics tutorial for
residents: General overview of fluoroscopic imaging. Radiographics 2000;20[4]:1115-

Figure 6 Schematic illustrations show three fluoroscopic geometries. A, The x-ray tube is
too close to the patient, which is indicated by the large change in ray spacing between
the entrance to and exit from the patient (ray spacing is related to the dose rate). B, The
x-ray tube is farther from the patient, and the dose distribution is more uniform;
however, the image intensifier tube is too far from the patient, which increases the
patient entrance dose. C, Both tubes are placed appropriately. (Reproduced with
permission from Brateman L: Radiation safety considerations for diagnostic radiology
personnel. Radiographics 1999;19[4]:1037-1055.)
With fluoroscopy, everyone in the room must wear a lead apron during equipment use.
Thyroid shields and protective goggles also are recommended. Placement of the
operator’s hands in direct exposure of the x-ray beam should be avoided.
Operators should image intermittently rather than have a lead foot and take advantage
of the last-image-hold feature, in which the last image obtained remains on the monitor
after x-ray exposure is terminated. To further decrease irradiation, pulsed fluoroscopy,
in which the x-ray beam is emitted as a series of short pulses rather than as continuous
irradiation output, is commonly used. Automatic exposure rate control maintains the
irradiation dose per frame rate at a preset level (accounting for attenuation
characteristics of a patient’s body habitus) and maintains a consistent level of image

18/26

quality. Added aluminum and/or copper beam hardening filters between the x-ray tube
and the collimator reduce skin entrance dose.
In addition to general training with fluoroscopic equipment, orthopaedic surgeons also
may benefit from procedure-specific training. For example, in the placement of
intramedullary nails, the insertion of locking screws is difficult, often requiring long
imaging times with resultant high irradiation doses. Specific training in this procedure
would lead to more timely and accurate insertion of the locking screws because the C-
arm must be precisely positioned over the nail so that each screw hole appears as a
perfect circle.4 Armed with this knowledge and experience, the operator would
understand that if the C-arm is properly positioned, the x-ray beam marks the direction
of drilling for the orthopaedic surgeon, thereby reducing procedure time and irradiation
dose.
The use of an in-field fixed object that serves as a template is recommended because
distortion is a known intrinsic error associated with image-intensified fluoroscopy15
(Resource 14).
An orthopaedic surgery simulation performed to evaluate contamination from the C-arm
drape during intraoperative fluoroscopy discovered that frequent repositioning of the C-
arm to obtain lateral images resulted in secondary contamination of the surgical field16
(Resource 15). The clip drape technique for lateral fluoroscopy has been shown to
reduce contamination rates17 (Resource 16).
EOS Imaging
EOS imaging is a low-dose technique.
No cranio-caudal magnification or distortion
This technique can be used to assess the entire skeleton and is particularly useful in evaluating
spine deformity, limb-length discrepancy, and lower extremity alignment.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Radiography and Fluoroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000502
19/26


EOS Imaging
The EOS imaging system is a new, advanced x-ray technology that reduces irradiation
exposure and images without length distortion/magnification. The EOS imaging system
is named after the company that developed the technology (EOS Imaging); it is not an
acronym. The EOS imaging system consists of two pairs of perpendicular linked x-ray
tubes that move vertically and horizontally, producing x-ray beams collected by
detectors6,18 (Figure 7; Resource 5). These detectors can capture more photons than
conventional x-ray detectors; therefore, fewer x-rays are required to produce the
images. EOS imaging is a weight-bearing technique that can simultaneously obtain full
body images of the skeletal system in frontal and lateral projections. This low-dose
technique is a reasonable alternative to radiography in the interest of minimizing
ionizing irradiation exposure in pediatric patients, especially those with chronic skeletal
conditions requiring periodic follow-up, while maintaining the accuracy of diagnostic
measures19 (Resource 17).
Figure 7 Illustrations show the operational principles of the EOS two-dimensional/three-
dimensional imaging system. Perpendicularly placed, vertically moving, co-linked units of
x-ray tubes producing very thin collimated x-ray beams collected by unique line
detectors with Nobel Prize–winning technology (A) result in simultaneously captured
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Radiography and Fluoroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000502
20/26

biplanar digital images of a patient in a standing, weight-bearing position (B). (Courtesy
of EOS Imaging, Paris, France).
Performed with the patient in various positions, the EOS imaging system also can
provide functional radiographic information and can be processed to produce three-
dimensional reconstruction images of the entire body18 (Figure 8). This is especially
useful for preoperative planning because anatomic structures are represented true to
size. In total hip arthroplasty, for example, spatially calibrated AP and lateral static views
in standing, squatting, and sitting positions can be obtained in seconds at a fraction of
the irradiation dose used for plain radiography6 (Resource 5). These functional images
are important in determining the hip-spine relationship in total hip arthroplasty. In
addition, three-dimensional reconstruction models can be used to determine acetabular
positioning relative to the changes in lumbar and pelvic alignment in various positions.
The utility of the EOS imaging system is limited in patients with periprosthetic loosening
and osteolysis.
